claim: The gut has built a physical, chemical, microbial, and immune barrier to protect the body against pathogen invasion.
source: As the largest mucosal surface, the gut has built a physical, chemical, microbial, and immune barrier to protect the body against pathogen invasion.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about gut barrier function.

claim: The disturbance of gut microbiota aggravates pathogenic bacteria invasion and gut barrier injury.
source: The disturbance of gut microbiota aggravates pathogenic bacteria invasion and gut barrier injury.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing prior research.

claim: FMT regulated gut microbiota and enhanced the protection of AIMD piglets against ETEC K88 challenge.
source: The results showed that FMT regulated gut microbiota and enhanced the protection of AIMD piglets against ETEC K88 challenge, as demonstrated by reduced intestinal pathogen colonization and alleviated gut barrier injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the piglet study showing reduced pathogen colonization and improved barrier function.

claim: Akkermansia muciniphila and Bacteroides fragilis were identified as two strains that may play key roles in FMT.
source: Akkermansia muciniphila (A. muciniphila) and Bacteroides fragilis (B. fragilis) were identified as two strains that may play key roles in FMT.
evidence: This is based on LEfSe analysis of microbiome sequencing data showing these strains were significantly changed after FMT.

claim: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis relieved ETEC-induced intestinal inflammation by maintaining the proportion of Treg/Th17 cells.
source: We further investigated the alleviatory effects of these two strains on ETEC infection in the AIMD mice model, which revealed that A. muciniphila and B. fragilis relieved ETEC-induced intestinal inflammation by maintaining the proportion of Treg/Th17 cells and epithelial damage by moderately activating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, while the effect of A. muciniphila was better than B. fragilis.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing changes in Treg and Th17 cell proportions in mice treated with these bacteria.

claim: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis relieved epithelial damage by moderately activating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway.
source: We further investigated the alleviatory effects of these two strains on ETEC infection in the AIMD mice model, which revealed that A. muciniphila and B. fragilis relieved ETEC-induced intestinal inflammation by maintaining the proportion of Treg/Th17 cells and epithelial damage by moderately activating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, while the effect of A. muciniphila was better than B. fragilis.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and RT-qPCR data showing modulation of Wnt pathway components.

claim: The effect of A. muciniphila was better than B. fragilis in relieving ETEC-induced damage.
source: We further investigated the alleviatory effects of these two strains on ETEC infection in the AIMD mice model, which revealed that A. muciniphila and B. fragilis relieved ETEC-induced intestinal inflammation by maintaining the proportion of Treg/Th17 cells and epithelial damage by moderately activating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, while the effect of A. muciniphila was better than B. fragilis.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of multiple parameters between A. muciniphila and B. fragilis treatment groups.

claim: A. muciniphila protected the intestinal stem cells and stimulated the proliferation and differentiation of intestinal epithelium.
source: A. muciniphila did protect the intestinal stem cells and stimulate the proliferation and differentiation of intestinal epithelium, and the protective effects of A. muciniphila were reversed by Wnt inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by organoid culture data showing increased Ki67+ cells, Lgr5 expression, and organoid formation efficiency.

claim: The protective effects of A. muciniphila were reversed by Wnt inhibitor.
source: A. muciniphila did protect the intestinal stem cells and stimulate the proliferation and differentiation of intestinal epithelium, and the protective effects of A. muciniphila were reversed by Wnt inhibitor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using Wnt-C59 inhibitor in organoid models showing loss of protective effects.

claim: A. muciniphila was identified as a key strain in FMT to promote the proliferation and differentiation of intestinal stem cells by mediating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway.
source: A. muciniphila was identified as a key strain in FMT to promote the proliferation and differentiation of intestinal stem cells by mediating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway.
evidence: This conclusion integrates data from microbiome analysis, mouse experiments, and organoid studies showing A. muciniphila's effects through Wnt signaling.

claim: Antibiotic treatment is the most drastic exposure leading to intestinal microbiota dysbiosis.
source: The most drastic exposure that leads to intestinal microbiota dysbiosis is antibiotic treatment, which kills commensal micro-organisms and inhibits these microbiota-mediated immune defense (Andremont et al., 2021; Buffie and Pamer, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on antibiotic effects on microbiota.

claim: Antibiotic treatment kills commensal micro-organisms and inhibits microbiota-mediated immune defense.
source: The most drastic exposure that leads to intestinal microbiota dysbiosis is antibiotic treatment, which kills commensal micro-organisms and inhibits these microbiota-mediated immune defense (Andremont et al., 2021; Buffie and Pamer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited references on antibiotic mechanisms.

claim: The disturbance of intestinal microbiota may lead to disruptions of the gut barrier and increase the susceptibility of the host to pathogenic microbes.
source: The disturbance of intestinal microbiota may lead to disruptions of the gut barrier and increase the susceptibility of the host to pathogenic microbes (Flint et al., 2012; Witkowski et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Early-life exposure to antibiotics leads to gut microbiota dysbiosis that can impair host immune system maturation.
source: Several clinical studies have demonstrated that early-life exposure to antibiotics leads to gut microbiota dysbiosis that can impair host immune system maturation (An et al., 2014; Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The negative impact of antibiotics on gut microbiota in early life may last for long periods throughout a lifetime, increasing the risk of gut diseases.
source: Furthermore, the negative impact of antibiotics on gut microbiota in early life may even last for long periods throughout a lifetime, increasing the risk of gut diseases (Francino, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ETEC K88 infection is a common cause of diarrhea in humans and animals.
source: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) K88 infection is a common cause of diarrhea in humans and animals (Dubreuil, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When ETEC adheres to intestinal epithelial cells, virulence factors interact with specific receptors to induce intestinal barrier injury and intestinal inflammatory responses.
source: When ETEC adheres to intestinal epithelial cells, virulence factors interact with specific receptors to induce intestinal barrier injury and intestinal inflammatory responses (Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: FMT is a therapeutic intervention for reconstructing gut microbiota in gastrointestinal inflammatory diseases.
source: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is a therapeutic intervention for reconstructing gut microbiota in gastrointestinal inflammatory diseases (Borody et al., 2019; Colman and Rubin, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on FMT applications.

claim: FMT has been successful in treating Clostridioides difficile infection and maintaining the gut barrier.
source: Since FMT has been successful in treating Clostridioides difficile infection and maintaining the gut barrier, the emerging investigation has been focused on other diseases (Quraishi et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Intestinal stem cell renewal is vital for the maintenance of the gut barrier.
source: Intestinal stem cell renewal is vital for the maintenance of the gut barrier (Beumer and Clevers, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mammalian intestinal epithelial cells are renewed approximately every 3–5 d with the migration of undifferentiated intestinal cells from the crypt to the top of the villi.
source: Mammalian intestinal epithelial cells are renewed approximately every 3–5 d with the migration of undifferentiated intestinal cells from the crypt to the top of the villi, accompanied by the differentiation of different types of epithelial cells (Luo et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The proliferation and differentiation of intestinal epithelium driven by intestinal stem cells is a necessary process for repairing intestinal barrier injury to prevent pathogen invasion.
source: The proliferation and differentiation of intestinal epithelium driven by intestinal stem cells, mainly crypt-base columnar cells expressing R-Spondin receptor Lgr5, is a necessary process for repairing intestinal barrier injury to prevent pathogen invasion (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Sato et al., 2009 successfully cultured isolated intestinal stem cells into three-dimensional intestinal organoids with villous and crypt-like structural morphology for the first time.
source: Sato et al., 2009 successfully cultured isolated intestinal stem cells into three-dimensional intestinal organoids with villous and crypt-like structural morphology for the first time.
evidence: This is a citation to a landmark study in organoid culture.

claim: Intestinal organoids contain various terminally differentiated cell types, including intestinal stem cell, tuft cell, absorptive cell, enteroendocrine cell, goblet cell, and Paneth cell.
source: Intestinal organoids contain various terminally differentiated cell types, including intestinal stem cell, tuft cell, absorptive cell, enteroendocrine cell, goblet cell, and Paneth cell, which have more advantages over single cell lines for in vitro study of intestinal regeneration (Sprangers et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on organoid composition.

claim: Intestinal organoid is an ideal model for studying the interaction between intestinal epithelium and microorganisms in vitro, which can eliminate the complexity of animal models.
source: Intestinal organoid is an ideal model for studying the interaction between intestinal epithelium and microorganisms in vitro, which can eliminate the complexity of animal models (Yin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on organoid applications.

claim: Co et al., 2019 first established the intestinal organoid model with polarity reversal in humans and mouse.
source: Co et al., 2019 first established the intestinal organoid model with polarity reversal in humans and mouse, which optimizes the shortcomings of microinjection in terms of heterogeneous exposure concentrations and durations, as well as destruction of organoid walls, and evaluated the infection effects of the invasive pathogens with different polarity-specific patterns.
evidence: This is a citation to a landmark study on polarity-reversed organoids.

claim: FMT decreased ADG and increased diarrhea scores in AIMD piglets on day 3 and day 6 after ETEC K88 infection were relieved by FMT treatment.
source: As shown in Figure 2A and B, decreased ADG and increased diarrhea scores were observed in AIMD piglets on day 3 and day 6 after ETEC K88 infection, and these symptoms were relieved by FMT treatment.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B measuring ADG and diarrhea scores.

claim: FMT significantly decreased the copies of ETEC K88 in the jejunal and colonic mucosa.
source: We next detected the pathogen colonization in mucosal tissues and found that FMT significantly decreased the copies of ETEC K88 in the jejunal and colonic mucosa (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: FMT decreased the expression of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) and increased levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10 and TGF-β1) in the jejunum.
source: FMT decreased the expression of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) and increased levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10 and TGF-β1) in the jejunum (p<0.01, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Jejunal scanning electron microscopy showed that the villi in ETEC K88 infected piglets were short and coarse, and there existed obvious rod-shaped bacterial adhesion on the surface of microvilli.
source: Jejunal scanning electron microscopy showed that the villi (Figure 3A top) in ETEC K88 infected piglets were short and coarse, and there existed obvious rod-shaped bacterial adhesion on the surface of microvilli (Figure 3A bottom), while FMT reversed villi and microvilli injury caused by ETEC K88.
evidence: This is supported by SEM images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: FMT reversed villi and microvilli injury caused by ETEC K88.
source: Jejunal scanning electron microscopy showed that the villi (Figure 3A top) in ETEC K88 infected piglets were short and coarse, and there existed obvious rod-shaped bacterial adhesion on the surface of microvilli (Figure 3A bottom), while FMT reversed villi and microvilli injury caused by ETEC K88.
evidence: This is supported by SEM images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The reduced mRNA and protein levels of the tight junctions (ZO-1, claudin, and occludin) and adherence junctions (β-catenin and E-cadherin) caused by ETEC K88 challenge were reversed by FMT treatment in the jejunum.
source: In addition, the reduced mRNA and protein levels of the tight junctions (ZO-1, claudin, and occludin) and adherence junctions (β-catenin and E-cadherin) caused by ETEC K88 challenge were also reversed by FMT treatment in the jejunum (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: ETEC K88 infection reduced the expression of MUC2, which was significantly increased following FMT administration.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, ETEC K88 infection reduced the expression of MUC2, which was significantly increased following FMT administration.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The alpha diversity indexes Chao1 and Observed species were increased after FMT treatment.
source: The alpha diversity indexes Chao1 and Observed species were increased after FMT treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by microbiome sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The PCoA and NMDS showed that gut microbiota between the two groups clustered separately.
source: The PCoA and NMDS showed that gut microbiota between the two groups clustered separately (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by beta diversity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: The Anosim analysis (R=0.396, p=0.02) indicated that FMT altered the structure of the gut microbiota in ETEC K88-challenged piglets.
source: The Anosim analysis (R=0.396, p=0.02) and UPGMA clustering analysis also indicated that FMT altered the structure of the gut microbiota in ETEC K88-challenged piglets (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by Anosim statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: LEfSe analysis verified that B. fragilis and Akkermansia were changed significantly with an upper 4 LDA score after FMT administration.
source: LEfSe analysis verified that B. fragilis and Akkermansia were changed significantly with an upper 4 LDA score after FMT administration (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The OTU sequence of Akkermansia was identified as A. muciniphila by comparison in the NCBI database using the Blast method.
source: We compared the OTU sequence of Akkermansia in the National Center for Biotechnology Information database by using the Blast method based on the Best Hit algorithm, and the result was A. muciniphila.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic sequence comparison.

claim: FMT significantly increased the production of SCFA metabolites, including acetic acid, propionic acid, butyric acid, isobutyric acid, isovaleric acid, and hexanoic acid.
source: Furthermore, FMT significantly increased the production of SCFA metabolites, including acetic acid, propionic acid, butyric acid, isobutyric acid, isovaleric acid, and hexanoic acid (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ETEC K88 infection led to weight loss and intestinal morphology damage, which was relieved by A. muciniphila and B. fragilis treatment.
source: As shown in (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), ETEC K88 infection led to weight loss and intestinal morphology damage, which was relieved by A. muciniphila and B. fragilis treatment.
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements and histological analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis increased the height and number of microvilli and ameliorated the distribution of intercellular junction in the jejunum and colon.
source: Correspondingly, scanning electron microscopy showed that A. muciniphila and B. fragilis increased the height and number of microvilli and ameliorated the distribution of intercellular junction in the jejunum and colon (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by TEM images shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The relative mRNA and protein expressions of MUC2 were significantly increased in the jejunum of A. muciniphila and B. fragilis-treated mice.
source: In addition, the relative mRNA and protein expressions of MUC2 were significantly increased in the jejunum of A. muciniphila and B. fragilis-treated mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Only A. muciniphila could upregulated MUC2 protein expression in the colon of treated mice.
source: However, only A. muciniphila could upregulated MUC2 protein expression in the colon of treated mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ETEC K88 infection surged the number of Escherichia coli in the feces, jejunum, colon, liver, spleen, and kidney.
source: ETEC K88 infection surged the number of Escherichia coli in the feces, jejunum, colon, liver, spleen, and kidney (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis treatment dramatically decreased the amount of ETEC K88 in tissues and organs.
source: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis treatment dramatically decreased the amount of ETEC K88 in these tissues (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating a reduced translocation of ETEC K88 in the tissues and organs.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis significantly decreased serum FD4 concentration, indicating enhanced intestinal barrier integrity.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, A. muciniphila, and B. fragilis significantly decreased serum FD4 concentration, indicating A. muciniphila and B. fragilis enhanced intestinal barrier integrity.
evidence: This is supported by FD4 permeability assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ETEC K88 decreased the relative mRNA expression of anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β and increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 and IFN-γ, which was reversed in A and B groups.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 6A, ETEC K88 decreased the relative mRNA expression of anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β and increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 and IFN-γ, which was reversed in A and B groups, indicating that A. muciniphila and B. fragilis ameliorated ETEC K88-induced intestinal inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ETEC K88 infection significantly decreased the proportion of Treg cells and mature dendritic cells and increased the proportion of Th17 cells.
source: ETEC K88 infection significantly decreased the proportion of Treg cells and mature dendritic cells and increased the proportion of Th17 cells, while oral administration of A. muciniphila or B. fragilis significantly reduced the proportion of Th17 cells and increased the proportion of mature dendritic cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Oral administration of A. muciniphila or B. fragilis significantly reduced the proportion of Th17 cells and increased the proportion of mature dendritic cells.
source: ETEC K88 infection significantly decreased the proportion of Treg cells and mature dendritic cells and increased the proportion of Th17 cells, while oral administration of A. muciniphila or B. fragilis significantly reduced the proportion of Th17 cells and increased the proportion of mature dendritic cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Compared with E group, the proportion of Treg cells in A group was significantly increased (p<0.01).
source: Moreover, compared with E group, the proportion of Treg cells in A group was significantly increased (p<0.01), and the proportion of Treg cells in the B group had an increasing trend (p=0.59), indicating FMT maintained the proportion of Treg/Th17 cells in ETEC K88-infected mice.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ETEC K88 infection prominently decreased Ki67 and Lyz mRNA expression and the number of Ki67+ cells and Lyz+ Paneth cells in the crypt of the jejunum.
source: ETEC K88 infection prominently decreased Ki67 and Lyz mRNA expression and the number of Ki67+ cells and Lyz+ Paneth cells in the crypt of the jejunum (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis increased Ki67 and Lyz mRNA expression and the number of Ki67+ cells.
source: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis increased Ki67 and Lyz mRNA expression and the number of Ki67+ cells.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Only A. muciniphila enhanced the number of Lyz+ Paneth cells.
source: However, only A. muciniphila enhanced the number of Lyz+ Paneth cells, suggesting that A. muciniphila accelerated the proliferation and differentiation of intestinal epithelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ETEC K88 infection significantly increased the relative mRNA expression of Lgr5, Wnt3, Axin2, Ctnnb1 in jejunum mucosa and had no significant impact on Notch1 and Hes1 expression.
source: ETEC K88 infection significantly increased the relative mRNA expression of Lgr5, Wnt3, Axin2, Ctnnb1 in jejunum mucosa and had no significant impact on Notch1 and Hes1 expression (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis inhibited the upregulation of Lgr5, Wnt3, Axin2, and Ctnnb1 at transcriptional level caused by ETEC K88 infection and had no significant effect on Notch1 and Hes1 levels.
source: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis inhibited the upregulation of Lgr5, Wnt3, Axin2, and Ctnnb1 at transcriptional level caused by ETEC K88 infection and had no significant effect on Notch1 and Hes1 levels.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A. muciniphila and B. fragilis inhibited the upregulation Lgr5, Wnt3, Active β-catenin, c-Myc, and CyclinD1 at protein level, and the effect of A. muciniphila was better than that of B. fragilis.
source: Western blot analysis also showed that A. muciniphila and B. fragilis inhibited the upregulation Lgr5, Wnt3, Active β-catenin, c-Myc, and CyclinD1 at protein level, and the effect of A. muciniphila was better than that of B. fragilis (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A. muciniphila regulated the expression of intestinal stem cells in ETEC K88-challenged mice and regulated Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway rather than Notch signaling pathway.
source: These results implied that A. muciniphila regulated the expression of intestinal stem cells in ETEC K88-challenged mice and regulated Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway rather than Notch signaling pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on Wnt versus Notch pathway components.

claim: In ETEC K88-infected mice, the crypts formed into undifferentiated spherical organoids, while in A. muciniphila or B. fragilis-treated mice, the crypts generated mature organoids with bud structure.
source: In ETEC K88-infected mice, the crypts formed into undifferentiated spherical organoids, while in A. muciniphila or B. fragilis-treated mice, the crypts generated mature organoids with bud structure (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by organoid culture images shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The organoids derived from ETEC K88-infected mice had a smaller surface area and lower forming efficiency than those from control mice.
source: As shown in Figure 8B, the organoids derived from ETEC K88-infected mice had a smaller surface area and lower forming efficiency than those from control mice.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A. muciniphila treatment led to a larger surface area and higher forming efficiency of the intestinal organoids.
source: A. muciniphila treatment led to a larger surface area and higher forming efficiency of the intestinal organoids.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The surface area of intestinal organoids in B group was larger than that in E group, while there was no significant difference in forming efficiency between these two groups.
source: The surface area of intestinal organoids in B group was larger than that in E group, while there was no significant difference in forming efficiency between these two groups.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The relative mRNA expression of villin, ZO-1, Ki67, Lyz, MUC2, Lgr5, Wnt3a, β-catenin in basal-out intestinal organoids were significantly down-regulated upon ETEC exposure.
source: The relative mRNA expression of villin, ZO-1, Ki67, Lyz, MUC2, Lgr5, Wnt3a, β-catenin and the fluorescence intensity of villin, Ki67, Lgr5, Wnt3a, and β-catenin in basal-out intestinal organoids were significantly down-regulated upon ETEC exposure (Figure 9A–G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 9A-G.

claim: A. muciniphila upregulated Lgr5, Wnt3a, and β-catenin expression in ETEC-infected organoids, while these effects were inhibited by Wnt-C59 treatment.
source: A. muciniphila upregulated Lgr5, Wnt3a, and β-catenin expression in ETEC-infected organoids, while these effects were inhibited by Wnt-C59 treatment (Figure 9A–G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 9A-G.

claim: A. muciniphila increased the number of intestinal stem cells and activated Wnt signaling, but did not promote the proliferation and differentiation of basal-out gut organoids.
source: The results suggested that A. muciniphila increased the number of intestinal stem cells and activated Wnt signaling, but did not promote the proliferation and differentiation of basal-out gut organoids.
evidence: This is inferred from the organoid data showing limited effects in basal-out configuration.

claim: Co-cultivation with A. muciniphila restored the epithelial barrier integrity of organoids challenged by ETEC K88.
source: We conducted FD4 permeation test in apical-out intestinal organoid model, and co-cultivation with A. muciniphila restored the epithelial barrier integrity of organoids challenged by ETEC K88 (Figure 10A and H).
evidence: This is supported by FD4 permeability assay data shown in Figures 10A and 10H.

claim: A. muciniphila increased the mRNA expression of ZO-1, Lyz, and MUC2 in the ETEC K88 infected apical-out intestinal organoids.
source: A. muciniphila not only increased the mRNA expression of ZO-1, Lyz, and MUC2 in the ETEC K88 infected apical-out intestinal organoids, but also up-regulated the protein expression of villin, Wnt3a, β-catenin, and the number of Lgr5+ and Ki67+ cells (Figure 10B-G, I).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: A. muciniphila up-regulated the protein expression of villin, Wnt3a, β-catenin, and the number of Lgr5+ and Ki67+ cells in apical-out organoids.
source: A. muciniphila not only increased the mRNA expression of ZO-1, Lyz, and MUC2 in the ETEC K88 infected apical-out intestinal organoids, but also up-regulated the protein expression of villin, Wnt3a, β-catenin, and the number of Lgr5+ and Ki67+ cells (Figure 10B-G, I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 10C-G and 10I.

claim: A. muciniphila relieved the inflammatory response of the ETEC K88 infected apical-out intestinal organoids by decreasing proinflammatory cytokines and increasing anti-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Moreover, A. muciniphila also relieved the inflammatory response of the ETEC K88 infected apical-out intestinal organoids, as determined by decreasing proinflammatory cytokines, inducing TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IFN-γ, and increasing anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β (Figure 10J).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 10J.

claim: The moderating effect of A. muciniphila on the apical-out intestinal organoids disappeared after Wnt-C59 exposure.
source: However, the moderating effect of A. muciniphila on the apical-out intestinal organoids disappeared after Wnt-C59 exposure.
evidence: This is supported by data showing loss of A. muciniphila effects when Wnt inhibitor is added.

claim: A. muciniphila accelerated the proliferation and differentiation of the intestinal stem cells and ameliorated the intestinal barrier injury and inflammation induced by ETEC K88.
source: Taken together, A. muciniphila accelerated the proliferation and differentiation of the intestinal stem cells and ameliorated the intestinal barrier injury and inflammation induced by ETEC K88.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the organoid experimental data.

claim: A. muciniphila protected intestinal organoids against ETEC infection via Wnt signaling.
source: A. muciniphila protected intestinal organoids against ETEC infection via Wnt signaling.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the reversal of protective effects by Wnt inhibitor.

claim: A. muciniphila utilizes mucin as the only carbon and nitrogen source for its growth in the gut.
source: A. muciniphila utilizes mucin as the only carbon and nitrogen source for its growth in the gut, and its metabolite SCFAs can facilitate MUC2 secretion by goblet cells to maintain the dynamic balance of intestinal mucus layer (Ottman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on A. muciniphila metabolism.

claim: A. muciniphila metabolite SCFAs can facilitate MUC2 secretion by goblet cells to maintain the dynamic balance of intestinal mucus layer.
source: A. muciniphila utilizes mucin as the only carbon and nitrogen source for its growth in the gut, and its metabolite SCFAs can facilitate MUC2 secretion by goblet cells to maintain the dynamic balance of intestinal mucus layer (Ottman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A. muciniphila negatively correlated with many diseases, including diabetes, obesity, and inflammatory bowel diseases.
source: A. muciniphila negatively correlated with many diseases, including diabetes, obesity, and inflammatory bowel diseases (Belzer and de Vos, 2012; Castro-Mejía et al., 2016; Plovier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A. muciniphila effectively inhibited intestinal inflammatory response and elevated epithelial barrier function.
source: It has been reported that A. muciniphila effectively inhibited intestinal inflammatory response and elevated epithelial barrier function (Everard et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: B. fragilis could decompose mucin by lipid-anchored enzymes and interact with intestinal epithelial cells, thereby altering intestinal permeability and repairing intestinal epithelial barrier.
source: B. fragilis could decompose mucin by lipid-anchored enzymes and interact with intestinal epithelial cells, thereby altering intestinal permeability and repairing intestinal epithelial barrier (Donaldson et al., 2016; Hsiao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: B. fragilis altered macrophage phenotype and increased the phagocytosis of macrophages to restrain pathogens colonization.
source: Deng et al., 2016 reported that B. fragilis altered macrophage phenotype and increased the phagocytosis of macrophages to restrain pathogens colonization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Ki67 is widely expressed in proliferating cells and presents a reliable indicator of cell proliferation activity.
source: Ki67 is widely expressed in proliferating cells and presents a reliable indicator of cell proliferation activity (Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Ki67 reaches its peak during the division stage with short half-life period and easy degradation.
source: Ki67 reaches its peak during the division stage with short half-life period and easy degradation (Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Paneth cells produce antimicrobial peptides and express key niche signals that regulate stem cells.
source: Paneth cells not only produce antimicrobial peptides and express key niche signals that regulate stem cells, but also secrete activators that dynamically modulate Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway (Hou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.
